cues.text: In Nagasaki, one in three people is over sixty-five.
Here, the hardest part of the day is often a small one.
And asking a neighbour can feel like a burden.
The helpers already live here. Nothing connects them.
Otagai. It means, mutual. Help is close by.
First, join your circle. The people in your building, approved by your circle leader.
See what neighbours can lend, and what they're happy to help with.
Tanaka-san just says what she needs. Otagai writes it as a polite request. Nothing is sent until she taps send.
It starts with family, then widens, gently. No reply is a quiet no.
Rahim reads it in Bengali. His reply reaches her in Japanese. Then they meet, in person.
Now Rahim wants to put up a shelf. He doesn't know the tool. He just shows the wall.
Tanaka-san has the drill. One photo becomes a listing, and they check the parts together.
There are no star ratings here. Only thank-yous, and a quiet record that help goes both ways.
With their permission, family can ask on someone's behalf. Even Rahim's mother, back home in Cumilla.
Circle notices and cleaning days reach every neighbour, in their own language.
And on the hardest day, the same circle checks on each other. One tap. I'm safe, or I need help. Leaders see who needs a hand first.
AI suggests. People decide. Contact details stay private, and anyone can report or block.
Nagasaki already has the helpers. Otagai is the connection.
